paragraphs: Large recommendation systems process enormous streams of user actions and many different kinds of features, yet increasing their computing budget often fails to improve conventional models proportionally. This paper revisits that design problem by treating recommendation as sequential transduction within a generative framework: learning from action sequences to produce recommendations.

The proposed HSTU architecture is designed for streaming recommendation data with many distinct feature values and patterns that change over time. On synthetic and public datasets, it improves NDCG by up to 65.8% over baselines. For sequences of length 8,192, it runs 5.3 to 15.2 times faster than Transformers using FlashAttention2.

At 1.5 trillion parameters, HSTU-based recommenders improve online A/B-test metrics by 12.4% and have been deployed across multiple surfaces of a platform serving billions of users. The authors also observe power-law improvement with training compute across three orders of magnitude. These empirical results support a path toward more scalable recommendation models, while the proposed connection to recommendation foundation models remains a future direction.
icml-2024-actions-speak-louder-than-word.tldr: HSTU recasts recommendation as generative sequence modeling, delivering reported gains in quality, speed, and scaling with training compute.

paragraphs: Estimating how an outcome changes with a continuously varying treatment becomes difficult when the outcome is only partly observed. If outcome availability depends on measured covariates, restricting analysis to complete cases can introduce selection bias. The paper studies how additional observations can help address this problem.

Its additional information comes from surrogates: fully observed variables measured after treatment that are related to the primary outcome. The authors propose a doubly robust estimator that incorporates these variables and uses both examples with observed outcomes and examples without them. This makes the unlabeled portion of the data useful for estimating treatment effects, rather than discarding it.

The paper establishes asymptotic normality for the proposed estimator and reports that it avoids the selection-bias problem described in the setting. It also shows that incorporating surrogates can reduce variance relative to methods using labeled data alone; this is a possible improvement, not an unconditional guarantee. Extensive simulations support the method’s empirical performance.
icml-2024-continuous-treatment-effects-w.tldr: A doubly robust estimator uses surrogate outcomes and unlabeled data to estimate continuous treatment effects while addressing selection bias.

paragraphs: Teams in sequential adversarial games may need to coordinate before play even though their members later possess different information. Computing an optimal coordinated strategy is difficult because the available strategy space grows exponentially with the game tree. Column generation addresses this by adding useful strategies incrementally through a best-response oracle.

A Team Belief Directed Acyclic Graph, or TB-DAG, provides another representation of coordinated strategies, but it can still be exponentially large. Directly running the oracle on that representation therefore creates a scalability problem. The proposed DCG framework instead computes a coordinated best response in the original game and then converts that strategy into TB-DAG form.

The authors further develop an oracle that reduces conversion costs at each iteration. They theoretically establish exponentially faster convergence than state-of-the-art column-generation algorithms and report experimental speeds at least two orders of magnitude above the tested baselines. The contribution combines the graph representation with incremental strategy discovery without requiring the best-response computation to operate directly on the full TB-DAG.
icml-2024-dag-based-column-generation-fo.tldr: DCG accelerates adversarial team-game solving by finding best responses in the original game before converting them into a graph representation.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends on useful positive examples: different samples that should receive related representations. Creating those examples is difficult across domains. Hand-designed augmentations require domain expertise and can change a sample’s meaning, while generative augmentation methods often depend on supervised data or large external datasets.

DiffAug couples a semantic encoder with a conditional diffusion model to generate positive examples without supervision. The encoder supplies a representation of a sample’s meaning, and the diffusion model generates new samples conditioned on that representation. These generated positives then support contrastive training, connecting the augmentation mechanism directly to the representation being learned.

The encoder and diffusion model undergo iterative training, allowing representation learning and positive-sample generation to improve together. Experiments on DNA sequences, visual data, and biological feature datasets show improvements over hand-designed and state-of-the-art model-based augmentation methods. The findings support the approach across the tested domains, with its central contribution being an unsupervised way to learn augmentations instead of specifying them through domain-specific rules.
icml-2024-diffaug-enhance-unsupervised-c.tldr: DiffAug jointly trains a semantic encoder and conditional diffusion model to generate useful positive examples for unsupervised contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Differentiable annealed importance sampling, or DAIS, allows optimization of the initial distribution used by annealed importance sampling. This paper asks what that learned starting distribution represents. Its central result connects the optimization procedure to fitting a tractable, parameterized approximation of a target distribution that is difficult to handle directly.

The theoretical connection holds in the limit of many transitions. In that limit, the authors characterize DAIS as minimizing a symmetric divergence between the initial and target distributions, described in the abstract as Jensen–Shannon divergence. This gives DAIS a variational-inference interpretation: its starting distribution can itself serve as the approximation of interest.

The authors test that interpretation on synthetic and real-world data by evaluating the learned initial distribution as a variational distribution. They find that it often estimates uncertainty more accurately than standard reverse-KL variational inference, importance-weighted variational inference, and forward-KL Markovian score climbing. The finding concerns the usefulness of the learned distribution, while the limiting theoretical result specifically depends on having many transitions.
icml-2024-differentiable-annealed-import.tldr: DAIS has a variational-inference interpretation in the many-transition limit, and its learned initial distribution often improves empirical uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Graph rationalization explains a graph classifier’s prediction by selecting a concise subset of the original graph. However, a small explanation is not automatically reliable: both the prediction and its selected rationale can depend on shortcuts in the data. Existing methods that counter these shortcuts have largely studied centralized datasets.

FedGR brings this problem into federated learning, where the method must address shortcuts associated with individual clients. It introduces two data augmenters that produce client-specific samples conflicting with those shortcuts. These examples are intended to weaken the usefulness of shortcut information during learning and help the model produce more meaningful rationales.

The approach matters because explainability and shortcut resistance are treated as connected learning problems within the federated setting. Rather than relying solely on concise graph subsets, it changes the training examples used to learn those subsets and predictions. Experiments on real-world benchmarks and synthetic datasets support FedGR’s effectiveness in federated learning. The stated result is mitigation of shortcut reliance, rather than a guarantee that every explanation is shortcut-free.
icml-2024-federated-self-explaining-gnns.tldr: FedGR uses client-specific augmentations that conflict with shortcuts to improve graph rationalization in federated learning.

paragraphs: Mixup creates synthetic training examples by interpolating between existing examples and their labels. For graphs, deciding what lies between two examples is difficult because graphs do not naturally share an ordinary Euclidean space. The paper argues that neglecting the geometry of this interpolation can produce inconsistent synthetic graph-label pairs.

GeoMix defines a shared space using Gromov–Wasserstein distance and maps input graphs into it through transformations that preserve their equivalence. The authors show that linear interpolation between transformed graphs traces a geodesic connecting the original graphs on the corresponding manifold. This supplies a geometric basis for keeping generated samples consistent with their mixed labels.

To make the approach more practical, the paper also introduces an accelerated algorithm operating on an approximate, lower-dimensional Gromov–Wasserstein manifold. Experiments show improvements in graph neural networks’ generalization and robustness. The contribution therefore combines a justification for graph interpolation with an approximation designed to make that interpolation usable in training, rather than treating graph mixing as an arbitrary combination of structures.
icml-2024-graph-mixup-on-approximate-gro.tldr: GeoMix gives graph mixup a geometric foundation and uses a lower-dimensional approximation to improve GNN generalization and robustness.

paragraphs: State entropy maximization encourages a reinforcement-learning agent to visit a diverse range of states. Much existing work assumes that the agent observes the system’s state directly. With partial observations, however, variety in sensor readings can differ substantially from variety in the underlying states, making observation entropy an unreliable substitute.

This paper targets entropy over the true states while restricting the policy to information available through partial observations. The resulting problem generalizes POMDPs and is intractable in general. The authors therefore develop a policy-gradient method for a first-order relaxation formulated on belief states, which represent uncertainty about the hidden system state.

The method is designed to use memory and computation efficiently. Alongside the algorithm, the paper provides formal characterizations of approximation gaps, the optimization landscape, and a hallucination problem. These analyses help distinguish the relaxed objective from the original exploration goal. The contribution is an approach to exploration under partial observability, with its computational tractability coming through a relaxation rather than an exact solution to the general problem.
icml-2024-how-to-explore-with-belief-sta.tldr: A belief-based policy-gradient method approximates true-state entropy maximization when agents can observe the environment only partially.

paragraphs: Offline imitation learning often has to work with imperfect demonstrations because expert examples are scarce. A central challenge is deciding which behaviors in noisy data are worth copying. Methods that select examples by their similarity to expert state-action pairs can overlook useful behaviors that take a different route.

This paper selects behaviors according to the states they produce. Judging an action through its resulting state explicitly incorporates information about the environment’s dynamics and allows useful departures from the expert demonstrations to be retained. The authors then introduce a lightweight behavior-cloning algorithm designed to use the expert examples together with the selected data.

The method is evaluated on complex, high-dimensional benchmarks covering continuous control and vision-based tasks. It outperforms existing methods on 20 of 21 benchmarks, typically by factors of two to five, while keeping runtime comparable to behavior cloning. These findings support the paper’s central idea: useful imitation data can be recognized through the consequences of behavior, even when that behavior differs from the available expert examples.
icml-2024-how-to-leverage-diverse-demons.tldr: Selecting demonstrations by their resulting states helps offline imitation learning recover useful behaviors beyond those resembling the expert.

paragraphs: Matrix multiplication accounts for a large share of deep-learning computation. Low-bit integers can make it more efficient, but approximating matrix entries introduces rounding errors. The authors first find that, without a low-bit restriction, integer matrix multiplications achieve parity with floating-point computation during training and inference for a variety of Transformer models.

The remaining difficulty is that a few large entries require more bits even when most entries fit into a small integer range. IM-Unpack addresses these heavy hitters by expanding a matrix into a larger representation whose entries all fit within an arbitrarily low-bit integer range. Low-bit matrix multiplications can then recover the original integer multiplication exactly.

This exactness concerns the original integer matrix operation, avoiding additional approximation from forcing its large entries into the smaller range. The tradeoff is extra operations caused by unpacking. The authors report that this overhead is small for many popular models, suggesting a route to exploiting low-bit computation while preserving the original integer result.
icml-2024-im-unpack-training-and-inferen.tldr: IM-Unpack expands integer matrices so arbitrarily low-bit multiplications can reproduce their original multiplication exactly, at an added computational cost.

paragraphs: Image restoration needs a mapping from a degraded image to a high-quality image, whereas diffusion generation commonly maps noise into data. This paper introduces the Generalized Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Bridge, or GOUB, to make the connection between low-quality and high-quality images central to the diffusion process.

The construction uses the generalized Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process’s tendency to move back toward its mean. A Doob’s h-transform then removes the variance of its steady-state distribution, enabling point-to-point diffusion mappings. The authors also connect several bridge models mathematically, showing that they can be expressed as special cases of GOUB. This gives the proposed method a unifying role as well as a restoration role.

The paper additionally introduces a corresponding Mean-ODE model intended to capture fine pixel detail and perceptual structure. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for both models across inpainting, deraining, and super-resolution. The abstract’s optimality claim is supported empirically, so the reported success concerns the evaluated restoration settings rather than a universal mathematical guarantee of best possible image recovery.
icml-2024-image-restoration-through-gene.tldr: GOUB constructs point-to-point diffusion bridges for image restoration and reports state-of-the-art results alongside a corresponding Mean-ODE model.

paragraphs: Event-sequence forecasting must predict both what happens and how much time passes between events. Neural temporal point processes are a common framework for this task, but their sequential structure can hamper long-horizon forecasting. This paper instead uses diffusion generation to predict multiple future events from a historical event sequence.

The model directly learns a joint distribution over future event types and the intervals between them. It contains two diffusion processes: one handles time intervals, and the other handles event categories. Their denoising functions can access intermediate representations from both processes, allowing predictions about timing and event identity to inform each other.

This interaction is the key distinction from treating the two kinds of output separately. The sequence-to-sequence formulation also makes multi-step forecasting part of the model’s direct objective. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for long-horizon temporal point-process forecasting. The results support jointly modeling timing, categories, and their interactions when predicting an extended sequence of future events.
icml-2024-interacting-diffusion-processe.tldr: Two interacting diffusion processes jointly forecast event types and time intervals, improving reported long-horizon event-sequence predictions.

paragraphs: Reward functions tell a robot which behavior to pursue, but designing them remains a bottleneck for learning many skills. Language models contain task knowledge that could help, yet their proposed rewards can be too imprecise to guide learning effectively. This paper grounds those proposals using feedback from execution.

The method first asks a language model to propose reward features and a parameterized reward function. It then updates the parameters through iterative self-alignment. Specifically, it reduces disagreement between the language model’s rankings and those produced by the learned reward function, using execution feedback as the basis for this comparison.

This creates a way to refine rewards without human involvement in the proposed process. Validation covers nine tasks across two simulation environments, where the method consistently improves training efficacy and efficiency. It also uses significantly fewer GPT tokens than an alternative based on reward mutations. The findings support parameter refinement guided by ranking agreement as an efficient way to turn language-model task knowledge into rewards grounded in the evaluated environments.
icml-2024-learning-reward-for-robot-skil.tldr: The method refines language-model-proposed robot rewards through execution-based ranking agreement, improving simulated training while using fewer GPT tokens.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was included in a model’s training data. Such tests help assess whether a trained model exposes information about its training set. This paper introduces RMIA, a statistical attack designed to make these assessments accurate without requiring many expensive reference models.

RMIA refines the null-hypothesis modeling used in likelihood-ratio tests and draws on both reference models and samples from a reference population. These two sources provide evidence for the membership decision. The contribution lies in how that evidence is combined into a test with low computational overhead and strong detection power.

The authors report higher test power than prior methods throughout the true-positive versus false-positive tradeoff, including evaluated points with zero false positives. RMIA also performs strongly with as few as one pretrained reference model and when other attack elements, such as data distribution, vary. These results support practical privacy-risk assessment under limited resources; an observed zero-false-positive operating point is an empirical result rather than a universal guarantee.
icml-2024-low-cost-high-power-membership.tldr: RMIA combines reference models and population samples in a statistical membership test that remains effective under tight computational budgets.

paragraphs: Integrated Gradients assigns importance to input features to help explain a model’s prediction. In vision applications, its visualizations can be noisy, and its attributions can be vulnerable to targeted attacks. This paper investigates whether choosing an attribution path that better reflects the data’s geometry can improve these explanations.

The method adapts path-based attribution to follow geodesics on a Riemannian data manifold. In plain terms, it computes attribution along paths that respect the curved structure of the data. Deep generative models are used in experiments on several real-world image datasets to study this geometry-aware version of Integrated Gradients.

The experiments show explanations that are more perceptually intuitive and substantially more robust to targeted attributional attacks. The findings concern the reliability of the explanation itself: changing the attribution path can affect how clearly and stably the method identifies relevant features. The paper therefore connects a geometric choice inside the explanation procedure to improvements in both visual interpretability and resistance to manipulation in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-manifold-integrated-gradients-.tldr: Following the data manifold’s geodesics makes Integrated Gradients explanations more perceptually intuitive and more resistant to targeted attribution attacks.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across tasks to improve learning on future tasks. A theoretical framework must therefore describe what gets transferred and how that transfer affects generalization. Previous PAC-Bayesian approaches represented this transfer indirectly by learning prior distributions over models, limiting the mechanisms that could be expressed within their analyses.

This paper develops new generalization bounds that describe meta-learning more directly as learning the learning algorithm itself. The object carried forward to future tasks can therefore be the procedure used to learn from them. This expands the framework’s flexibility beyond representing shared knowledge only through a learned model prior.

The authors argue that the framework can analyze a wide range of existing meta-learning mechanisms and help design new ones. They also report empirical improvements in prediction quality for practical meta-learning mechanisms. The theoretical and experimental contributions address complementary questions: how to reason about more varied forms of knowledge transfer, and whether mechanisms developed within that broader view can improve predictions in practice.
icml-2024-more-flexible-pac-bayesian-met.tldr: New PAC-Bayesian bounds frame meta-learning as learning a learning algorithm, allowing more flexible knowledge transfer across tasks.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online imitation learning first learns behavior from a fixed demonstration dataset and then improves it through limited environmental interaction. Simply joining existing offline and online methods can go wrong at this transition. The paper identifies a mismatch between the pretrained policy and the discriminator used to guide online learning.

When that discriminator starts with random, incompatible behavior, it can give misleading training signals and cause the policy to lose knowledge gained during pretraining. OLLIE addresses the mismatch by learning both a near-expert initial policy and an aligned initial discriminator. Preparing them together is intended to make the move into online imitation learning smooth and fast.

Across 20 challenging tasks spanning continuous control and vision-based domains, OLLIE consistently and significantly outperforms the tested baselines in performance, demonstration efficiency, and convergence speed. The findings emphasize that successful pretraining transfer depends on the initialization of the learning signal as well as the policy. In these experiments, aligning both components helps preserve useful behavior while enabling further improvement through interaction.
icml-2024-ollie-imitation-learning-from-.tldr: OLLIE jointly initializes an imitation policy and its discriminator to prevent disruptive offline-to-online transfer and accelerate finetuning.

paragraphs: Predictions about how often elements will be accessed can help a dictionary data structure organize its work more efficiently. The challenge is retaining dependable performance when those predictions are inaccurate. This paper introduces RobustSL, a skip-list-based dictionary augmented with predicted access frequencies, and studies both its benefits and its safeguards.

With suitable predictions, RobustSL achieves static optimality, which the paper identifies as optimal consistency. At the same time, each operation retains a logarithmic running-time guarantee even when predictions are generated adversarially. The two guarantees address different cases: useful predictions improve performance, while misleading predictions do not remove the stated worst-case protection.

The authors present RobustSL as the first learning-augmented dictionary to combine optimal consistency and robustness. Its robustness guarantees extend beyond those available in the cited earlier structures. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets also show better performance than alternative data structures. Together, the theory and experiments support using access predictions while maintaining an explicit bound on the cost of individual operations.
icml-2024-robust-learning-augmented-dict.tldr: RobustSL exploits accurate access-frequency predictions while guaranteeing logarithmic operation time even under adversarial predictions.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning single-index models under squared loss in the agnostic setting, where the data need not be perfectly described by a model in the chosen class. The goal is an efficient algorithm whose loss stays within a constant factor of the best achievable loss in that class.

The authors provide such an algorithm for a range of input distributions, including log-concave distributions, and a broad class of monotone, Lipschitz link functions. Their analysis relies on a new local error-bound concept called alignment sharpness. This optimization property is the central technical ingredient connecting the learning algorithm to its approximation guarantee.

The result advances beyond earlier work on unknown link functions that either assumed realizability or lacked a constant-factor guarantee. The authors identify it as the first efficient agnostic learner with this approximation quality even for Gaussian inputs and any nontrivial link-function class. Its significance is a conditional theoretical guarantee under the stated distribution and function assumptions, with alignment sharpness potentially useful beyond this problem.
icml-2024-robustly-learning-single-index.tldr: Alignment sharpness enables efficient constant-factor agnostic learning of single-index models under specified distribution and link-function conditions.

paragraphs: Predictive coding provides a computational-neuroscience framework for inference and learning. This paper adapts it into Langevin Predictive Coding, or LPC, for training deep generative models. The key change is to make the inference procedure perform sampling, connecting predictive coding to a probabilistic learning objective.

LPC injects Gaussian noise into predictive-coding inference and uses an encoder network to initialize the process. Together, these changes yield an amortized Langevin sampling method that optimizes a tight variational lower bound. The authors also introduce lightweight preconditioning, inspired by Riemannian Langevin methods and adaptive stochastic gradient descent, to make sampling less sensitive to step size.

In benchmark experiments, LPC generates higher-quality samples and converges in a fraction of the stochastic-gradient training iterations used by the compared variational autoencoders. It matches or exceeds their performance on FID, diversity, and coverage. These results support combining encoder-based initialization with noisy iterative inference, while the reported iteration reduction specifically measures training iterations rather than establishing an equivalent reduction in total runtime.
icml-2024-sample-as-you-infer-predictive.tldr: LPC turns predictive-coding inference into Langevin sampling and reports improved generative quality with fewer training iterations than compared VAEs.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution reconstructs a high-resolution image from a lower-resolution input. Specialized operations can help recover different kinds of detail, but simply stacking them can make a model computationally expensive. SeemoRe addresses this tension by organizing specialized experts into a collaborative architecture designed for efficient super-resolution.

At a broad level, its experts focus on informative features associated with rank and spatial structure. The model then examines rank choice more closely through a mixture of low-rank experts. These levels of specialization are intended to capture distinct factors needed for reconstruction and uncover fine detail within the learned features.

The approach matters because specialization is built into how the model distributes its reconstruction work, instead of merely adding more disparate operations. The authors report an optimal performance outcome with minimal computational costs in efficient settings. The stated finding supports the proposed balance between detailed reconstruction and computational economy in that setting; it does not establish that one expert arrangement is universally optimal for every super-resolution problem.
icml-2024-see-more-details-efficient-ima.tldr: SeemoRe combines spatial and rank-focused experts, including low-rank mixtures, to recover image detail with low computational cost.

paragraphs: Machine learning can accelerate database operations such as indexing, cardinality estimation, and sorting. However, changing data distributions can erode those gains and sometimes make learned methods worse than conventional alternatives. This paper addresses the lack of theoretical understanding needed to judge their performance after deployment on dynamic datasets.

The authors develop a framework called distribution learnability and use it to characterize the performance of learned versions of these operations. Their bounds describe achievable behavior and the circumstances in which learned models can outperform non-learned methods. The focus is therefore on explaining the conditions behind an advantage, rather than assuming that training a model automatically produces one.

The paper presents this as the first known theoretical characterization covering these learned operations in dynamic datasets. Its contribution is a set of guarantees and analytical tools for reasoning about performance as datasets change. These results provide a foundation for future analysis of learned database systems and help connect observed speed benefits with a more explicit account of when those benefits are achievable.
icml-2024-theoretical-analysis-of-learne.tldr: Distribution learnability provides theoretical bounds explaining when learned database operations can outperform conventional methods as data distributions change.

paragraphs: Unmeasured confounders can prevent observational data from determining a single causal effect. Partial identification instead seeks a range of effects compatible with the available information. This paper asks how much knowing the marginal distribution of an unmeasured confounder can narrow that range, without relying on additional auxiliary variables.

For discrete confounders, the authors derive closed-form, tight identification regions for any possible marginal distribution P(U). They do not impose extra restrictions based on quantities such as entropy or mutual information. They also establish a necessary-and-sufficient criterion for deciding whether this marginal information yields a region different from the vanilla partial-identification region.

The analysis reveals a negative result: as the confounder’s number of possible values grows, marginal-distribution information contributes minimally to partial identification. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The paper therefore supplies both a precise way to use this information and a characterization of its limited value, showing why knowing a confounder’s overall distribution may still leave substantial uncertainty about causal effects.
icml-2024-tight-partial-identification-o.tldr: The paper derives tight causal-effect bounds from discrete confounder marginals and shows their contribution becomes minimal as confounder cardinality grows.

paragraphs: Tensor networks offer efficient representations of extremely high-dimensional objects, but choosing their structure is difficult. Existing structure-search algorithms are often manually designed heuristics, and the paper identifies dimensionality and local convergence as persistent obstacles. It investigates whether language models can help discover better search algorithms automatically.

The proposed tnGPS framework models aspects of how human researchers develop algorithms. An elaborate prompting pipeline guides a language model through repeated generation, refinement, and enhancement of tensor-network structure-search algorithms. The object being improved is the search procedure itself, rather than just a single tensor-network structure.

In benchmark experiments, algorithms discovered through tnGPS outperform current state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the use of an iterative language-model workflow for algorithm discovery in this particular problem area. The contribution is both the discovery framework and evidence that its generated algorithms can be competitive: the language model participates in designing how the search is performed, reducing reliance on manually crafting each new heuristic.
icml-2024-tngps-discovering-unknown-tens.tldr: tnGPS uses iterative language-model prompting to discover tensor-network structure-search algorithms that outperform existing methods on evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment often uses preferences between complete responses, even though a model generates those responses one token at a time. This paper introduces Token-level Direct Preference Optimization, or TDPO, to bring the optimization closer to that sequential generation process and improve the balance between preference alignment and output diversity.

TDPO applies forward KL-divergence constraints at each token to regulate differences from a reference model. It uses the Bradley–Terry preference model in a token-based reward formulation while avoiding the need to train an explicit reward model. The approach aims to improve control over divergence throughout generation rather than handling alignment only at the full-response level.

Experiments across text tasks show a better alignment-diversity balance. In particular, TDPO improves that balance over DPO on controlled sentiment generation and single-turn dialogue datasets. The authors also report significantly better response quality than DPO and PPO-based reinforcement learning from human feedback. These findings support token-level divergence regulation as a useful design choice in the evaluated preference-learning tasks.
icml-2024-token-level-direct-preference-.tldr: TDPO regulates preference optimization at each token, improving the reported balance between human-preference alignment and generation diversity.
